questions.feedback: If you picked the thunder, that is the trap: Sound travels faster than light. Reteach point: we see the lightning flash before we hear the thunder because light is far faster than sound - the flash arrives almost instantly and the thunder follows seconds later.
questions.prompt: From a distant storm, what do you notice first?

questions.feedback: Rearrange the wave equation before substituting: wavelength = v / f. If you multiplied instead of dividing, your answer came out far larger than the speed - use the check 170 Hz x 2 m = 340 m/s to catch that.
questions.prompt: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with frequency 170 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.

choices.text: Light is transverse; sound is longitudinal
Light is longitudinal; sound is transverse
Both light and sound are longitudinal

questions.feedback: Light is the transverse wave: the vibration is across the direction of travel, like the dot bobbing up and down. Sound is longitudinal: the particles bunch and spread along the direction of travel.
questions.prompt: Which pair correctly describes light and sound waves?

questions.answer: Light is far faster than sound, so the flash from the strike arrives almost instantly while the thunder, travelling at only 340 m/s, follows seconds later.
questions.feedback: A strong answer compares the two speeds: light at about 300,000,000 m/s against sound at 340 m/s. An answer that only says 'light is fast' without the comparison means the speed gap - the whole reason for the delay - needs reteaching first next lesson.
questions.prompt: In one sentence: why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
